etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English desire (noun) and desiren (verb), from Old French desirer, desirrer, from Latin dēsīderō (“to long for, desire, feel the want of, miss, regret”), apparently from de- + sidus (in the phrase de sidere, "from the stars") in connection with astrological hopes. Compare consider and desiderate. Displaced native Old English wilnung (“desire”) and wilnian (“to desire”).

definitions.definition: To want; to wish for earnestly.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Exodus 34:24:
quote.text: Neither shall any man desire thy land.

quote.citation: 1874, Alfred Tennyson, “Lancelot and Elaine”, in Idylls of the King (The Works of Alfred Tennyson; VI), cabinet edition, London: Henry S. King & Co., […], →OCLC, page 88:
quote.text: [S]eeing you desire your child to live, / Thanks, but you work against your own desire;  […]

definitions.definition: To put a request to (someone); to entreat.

quote.citation: 1526, [William Tyndale, transl.], The Newe Testamẽt […] (Tyndale Bible), [Worms, Germany: Peter Schöffer], →OCLC, Acts:
quote.text: And when they founde no cause of deeth in hym, yet desired they Pilate to kyll him.

quote.citation: 1918, W[illiam] B[abington] Maxwell, chapter III, in The Mirror and the Lamp, Indianapolis, Ind.: The Bobbs-Merrill Company, →OCLC, page 15:
quote.text: Mr. Barrett, however, by fawning and flattery, seemed to be able to make not only Mrs. Churchill but everyone else do what he desired.

definitions.definition: To express a wish for; to entreat; to request.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, 2 Kings 4:28:
quote.text: Then shee said, Did I desire a sonne of my Lord ? did I not say, Doe not deceiue me?

quote.citation: c. 1603–1606, William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of King Lear”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene vii]:
quote.text: Desire him to go in; trouble him no more.

definitions.definition: To require; to demand; to claim.

quote.citation: c. 1580, Edmund Spenser, The Teares of the Muses:
quote.text: A doleful case desires a doleful song.

quote.citation: 1651–1653, Jer[emy] Taylor, ΕΝΙΑΥΤΟΣ [Eniautos]. A Course of Sermons for All the Sundays of the Year. […], 2nd edition, London:  […]  Richard Royston […], published 1655, →OCLC:
quote.text: She shall be pleasant while she lives, and desired when she dies.

definitions.definition: (uncountable) The feeling of desiring; an eager longing for something.

quote.citation: 1905, E. M. Forster, Where Angels Fear to Tread , chapter 7:
quote.text: He stood...filled with the desire that his son should be like him, and should have sons like him, to people the earth. It is the strongest desire that can come to a man - if it comes to him at all - stronger even than love or the desire for personal immortality.

quote.citation: 2013 June 7, David Simpson, “Fantasy of navigation”, in The Guardian Weekly, volume 188, number 26, page 36:
quote.text: It is tempting to speculate about the incentives or compulsions that might explain why anyone would take to the skies in [the] basket [of a balloon]: perhaps out of a desire to escape the gravity of this world or to get a preview of the next; […].

definitions.definition: (uncountable) Strong attraction, particularly romantic or sexual.
(uncountable) Motivation. (Can we add an example for this sense?)
